verses.translation_literal: And Jacob saw that there is grain in Egypt, and Jacob said to his sons, "Why do you look at one another?"
verses.translation_dramatic: The famine had settled over Canaan like a hand over a mouth. Jacob saw it: saw that in Egypt, far to the south, there was grain. And looking round the tent at his grown sons, standing there with their hands hanging, he said, sharply, "Why do you stand staring at one another?"
verses.directors_commentary:
Jacob "saw" something he could only have heard, which v. 2 admits ("I have heard"). Rashi takes it as a spark of prophetic insight; Radak, more plainly, that he saw people returning from the road with grain; Ibn Ezra, that Hebrew lets one sense stand for another, as when Isaac "sees" the smell of Jacob. Play it as an old man who finally lets himself notice what everyone else already knows.

The verb in his rebuke is a reflexive of "to see" (titra'u), literally "make yourselves seen / look at yourselves". The KJV's "look one upon another" is fair, but it flattens a real dispute. Rashi, Rashbam and Radak hear: why parade yourselves as if you had plenty while all the world goes down to buy? Sforno hears the paralysis of a committee in which each waits for another to move. Both colours work for the actors: the brothers are proud and stuck. Note too that the speech is addressed to his sons, not named: in this chapter Jacob is still the father who cannot let go of the ones he has.

philological_notes.note: A reflexive/reciprocal form of 'to see': 'show yourselves' or 'look at one another'. Rashi and Radak read it as making a show of well-being before others; Sforno as each looking to another to act.

token_glosses.gloss: do you look at one another

verses.translation_literal: And he said, "Look, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy for us from there, and we will live and not die."
verses.translation_dramatic: "Listen," he said. "I have heard it: there is grain in Egypt. Go down there. Buy for us from that place, and we shall live, and we shall not die."
verses.directors_commentary:
The speech is short and flat: no pleading, only the arithmetic of hunger. The last pair, "live and not die", is the oldest ring of covenant language, life against death, and it will return when Judah pleads in chapter 43. The KJV's "get you down thither" is archaic English for a plain imperative.

The verb "go down" (redu) is geographical truth: Egypt lies lower than the hill country. Rashi hears something else in it. He notes that Jacob says "go down" and not "go", and the numerical value of redu (reish-dalet-vav) is 210, the years Israel would later spend in Egypt. That is a rabbinic play and not the plain sense; keep it as an echo for the audience that knows the end of the story, not as something Jacob himself intends.

philological_notes.note: 'Go down.' The land of Egypt is entered by 'going down' from Canaan. Rashi sees a numerical hint of 210 years (reish 200 + dalet 4 + vav 6) in the form.
'That we may live and not die': life and death set side by side. Sforno reads it as survival at bare subsistence, not as plenty.

verses.translation_literal: And the brothers of Joseph went down, ten, to buy grain from Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: So they went down, ten men on the road south, the brothers of Joseph, to buy grain from Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The narrator does not say "the sons of Jacob" but "the brothers of Joseph", and the number "ten" is set apart. Rashi reads this as a hint that they regretted the sale and meant to deal with Joseph as a brother, ready to ransom him at any price; Radak sees the irony that by going down they are already fulfilling Joseph's dream. For the actors: they do not know who is waiting for them, but the audience does, and the title carries the whole weight.

The KJV's "buy corn in Egypt" has two flaws: "corn" in 1611 meant any grain, usually wheat or barley, never maize, and the Hebrew says "from Egypt" (mimitzrayim), the source of supply, not the place of purchase. A modern audience should hear a convoy of ten men and donkeys going to a state granary. Sforno adds a market detail: the seller would sell only to one household once, and not to many, lest they trade the grain on; so a family would send as many as it had to carry.

philological_notes.note: 'The brothers of Joseph', not 'sons of Jacob'. The choice of name frames the whole chapter around Joseph's absence.
Grain, here threshed grain for food; the verse pairs the verb lishbor 'to buy grain' with this noun, repeating the same sound.

verses.translation_literal: And [obj] Benjamin, brother of Joseph, Jacob did not send with his brothers, for he said, Lest harm happen to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: But Benjamin, the brother of Joseph, Jacob would not send down with the others. For he had said it aloud: let no harm meet him on the road.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sentence opens on the object, Benjamin, thrown to the front of the clause before the verb arrives. That is the Hebrew way of pointing a finger: ten went, but this one Jacob kept. Play it as a pause in the packing, a hand on one shoulder. Note the label "brother of Joseph". The narrator does not say "Jacob's son" or "the youngest": he names Benjamin by the lost brother, and Radak reads it as full brother, from the same father and mother, which is why the wound of Joseph is still open in Jacob's choice. The actors should hear Joseph's absence in every syllable.

The KJV's "sent not" and "Lest peradventure mischief befall him" are archaic and soft. Hebrew אָסוֹן (ason) is not "mischief", which in 1611 English was already weaker than the Hebrew; it is deadly harm, and Ibn Ezra glosses it simply as death. The same word returns in 42:38 and 44:29, where Jacob fears gray hairs going down to Sheol. The verb is קָרָא, "to meet, to happen upon": harm is imagined as something lying in wait on the road to run into him. Rashi (citing Genesis Rabbah) asks why harm would meet him on the road and not at home, and answers that the Accuser presses his case at the hour of danger. Radak notes that a road is where lions and thieves are found. Note too the tense: "for he said" reports Jacob's earlier statement; the narrator hands us the old man's fear as quoted speech.

For the ear of the time: the trip to Egypt is some 250 miles each way on foot or donkey, weeks of travel through open country with no law to protect a traveler, and a father with one surviving son of his beloved wife has reason to count that cost.

philological_notes.note: A rare word for fatal harm, used only here and in 42:38, 44:29 and Exodus 21:22-23. It means calamity that kills or nearly so, not minor mischief. Ibn Ezra glosses it as death.

From the root meaning 'to meet, to encounter'. Harm is pictured as something that runs into a man on the road. The ending -ennu is the energic form with 'him'. Rashi uses the verb to ask why harm would meet him on the road and not at home.
Here אֶת is the preposition 'with' (H0854), not the object marker found at the start of the verse. The two homophones frame the verse.

verses.translation_literal: And the sons of Israel came to buy grain in among those coming, for the famine was in the land of Canaan.
verses.translation_dramatic: They came to Egypt as part of a crowd, the sons of Israel, one more set of faces among the many who were coming to buy, for the famine lay on the land of Canaan.
verses.directors_commentary:
The narrator now calls them "the sons of Israel" (Jacob's second name) rather than "the brothers of Joseph": the ten arrive as the family of a patriarch who is also a nation in embryo. "In among those coming" says plainly that they were not alone: the famine drove many peoples to Egypt, and they stood in line. Radak reads that they did not stand apart because they were Hebrews but came among the other Canaanites; Sforno adds that travellers went in bands for safety against the bandits famine bred.

The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and Rashi add that Jacob told his sons to enter by different gates so the evil eye would not rest on ten fine, strong men; this is a later tradition, not in the Hebrew. The KJV is faithful here; its "corn" is again "grain". The important fact for the scene is that the famine is not Egypt's alone: it is regional, and Egypt, thanks to Joseph, has stores.

philological_notes.note: 'Sons of Israel'. The naming shifts from 'brothers of Joseph' (v. 3) to the sons of the patriarch as a group, anticipating the people.
'In among those coming'. Radak: they came with the crowd of other buyers from Canaan, not separately; Sforno: in bands, for safety.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph, he was the ruler over the land; he was the one who sold to all the people of the land. And the brothers of Joseph came and bowed down to him, faces to the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now Joseph was the master of the land. It was he, and no one lower, who sold grain to all the people of the land. And the brothers of Joseph came before him, and they bowed, and put their faces to the ground.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two emphatic pronouns, "he... he" (hu... hu), drive home that Joseph personally holds power and personally sells the grain. Ramban finds this odd for a viceroy and quotes the rabbis that all granaries but one were shut; Radak and Sforno give the practical reading: every buyer had to come before Joseph, who controlled sales by his seal or word, so the brothers could not avoid him. The word for ruler, shallit, is a rare title, Aramaic-sounding, which the Targums render the same way; the KJV's "governor" is acceptable.

Then the hinge: "they bowed down to him, face to the ground." The verb is the same that the dreams of chapter 37 used ("my sheaf stood up... and yours bowed down"). Rashi explains that this kind of bowing is full prostration with hands and feet stretched out. The KJV's "bowed down themselves... with their faces to the earth" is accurate but wordy. Let the actors fall completely flat; the audience should feel the dream closing on them.

philological_notes.note: 'The ruler, one with authority'. A rare title, Aramaic in flavour; here Joseph's standing as sole authority over the land.
'The one who sells grain', a causative participle of the root shavar 'to buy grain'; Ibn Ezra and Radak note it takes two objects.
Full prostration, faces to the ground, hands and feet stretched out, Rashi says; the same gesture the dreams had foretold.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph saw his brothers and he recognized them, and he made himself a stranger to them, and he spoke with them harsh things, and he said to them, "From where have you come?" And they said, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food."
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph looked, and there were his brothers, and he knew them at once. But he made himself a stranger to them. He put a hard edge on his voice and spoke to them roughly. "Where have you come from?" he said. "From the land of Canaan," they answered. "To buy food."
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is built on one root used twice: vayyakirem, "he recognized them", and vayyitnakker, "he made himself a stranger". The recognizer pretends to be a stranger; the KJV's "made himself strange" keeps this, though in modern English it sounds like "acted oddly". The Hebrew is exact: he turned himself into a foreigner (nokhri), so that the people who sold him as a slave are now standing in front of a man they take for an Egyptian. Ramban offers two readings: that Joseph disguised his appearance, as Jeroboam's wife did (1 Kgs 14), or that he only changed his manner of speech; Sforno says he dropped his usual humble courtesy, and fears being known by his voice.

He "spoke harsh things" (kashot), literally hard words, which the KJV softens to "spake roughly". Rashbam notes that his question "from where?" makes him look as if he did not know them. Remember also that, as Rashbam observes, he speaks through an interpreter (cf. 42:23), which helps the disguise. The brothers' answer is polite and complete, and so tells the audience that they still say nothing of the family.

philological_notes.note: The same root used twice: 'recognize' and 'make oneself a stranger'. The English must repeat the pattern to keep the wordplay; nokhri 'foreigner' belongs to the same family.
'Hard things': harsh words, stern talk. The KJV 'roughly' is an adverb for a Hebrew adjective used as an object; Ibn Ezra compares Proverbs 18:23.

token_glosses.gloss: and he made himself a stranger

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph knew his brothers. They did not know him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The same root a third time (vayyaker... hikkiruhu), now as a flat statement: one side knows, the other does not. The sentence is a mirror: "he knew them, and they, no, they knew him not." The KJV is right and cannot be improved, though "knew" for "recognized" can be misread as acquaintance in the biblical sense.

Why did they not know him? The text does not say. Rashi and Ramban cite the rabbis: he had left them beardless as a youth, and now stood before them bearded. Rashbam adds royal dress, the Egyptian language, and an interpreter. Radak: they could not imagine the slave they sold had become the master of Egypt. Ibn Ezra, reading the earlier verse, says he recognized them as a group first, then one by one. These are explanations of what the narrator leaves untold; the actor needs one of them, whichever suits the performance.

philological_notes.note: 'They recognized him', negated. Third use of the root nkr in two verses; the sentence plays the stranger/recognition theme out.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph remembered the dreams that he had dreamed about them, and he said to them, "Spies are you! To see the nakedness of the land you have come!"
verses.translation_dramatic: And Joseph remembered. The dreams came back, the sheaves bowing, the stars bowing, the dreams he had dreamed of them. "Spies," he said. "You are spies. You have come to see where the land lies bare."
verses.directors_commentary:
"Joseph remembered" is the narrator's only window into his mind in the whole scene, and he gives only this: the dreams. He gives no stated motive for what follows. Rashi: he knew the dreams had come true, since they bowed; Ramban argues the reverse, that only part of them had been fulfilled (Benjamin was missing, and the second dream needed the father), which would explain why he arranged the next steps. These are interpretations; the text states only that he remembered, then accused.

The accusation turns on 'ervat ha'aretz, "the nakedness of the land". The KJV keeps "nakedness" and so should we, because it is the word for private shame, the same used for exposed bodies in Leviticus 18. A spy sees the land's undefended places. Rashi and Rashbam take it as the breaches in the walls, where the country is easiest to conquer; Ibn Ezra, as the hidden secret of the land, like something one conceals. The BBE's "how poor the land is" is a paraphrase that loses the sexual image. Sforno adds that ten men together did not fit the pattern of ordinary buyers.

philological_notes.note: 'Nakedness of the land': the uncovered, undefended part. The word is used elsewhere for sexual nakedness; here it is the land's weak points. Rashi: where it is easy to conquer; Ibn Ezra: its hidden secret.
'Spies', a participle of the denominative verb from regel 'foot': those who go about on foot, scouting.
'He remembered': in Hebrew remembering moves one to act, not only to recall. The text gives no further explanation of his motive.

verses.translation_literal: And they said to him, "No, my lord! Your servants have come to buy food."
verses.translation_dramatic: "No, my lord," they said. "No. Your servants have come to buy food. Only food."
verses.directors_commentary:
The first thing out of the brothers' mouths is "No, my lord", and they call themselves "your servants", which is the language of men who bowed to the ground a moment ago and now stand accused of a capital offence. The irony is deliberate and heavy: the brothers who once hated the dreamer's claim to lordship now say 'adoni, "my lord", and 'avadekha, "your servants". They speak the dream without knowing it.

The small vav before "your servants" is rendered "but" by the KJV ("but to buy food are thy servants come"). Radak confirms the sense: the vav stands for "but", as in Psalm 7:5. The line is a flat denial followed by their purpose. Note that the verse has no hint of the money in the BBE ("with money"): that is an addition of the translator.

philological_notes.note: 'And your servants.' The vav is adversative ('but'), as Radak notes. The brothers use the language of the dreams, 'lord' and 'servants', without knowing it.

verses.translation_literal: "All of us are sons of one man, we. We are honest. Your servants have never been spies."
verses.translation_dramatic: "We are all sons of one man," they said. "We are honest men. Your servants are not, and have never been, spies."
verses.directors_commentary:
The brothers defend themselves with two arguments. The first, "all of us are sons of one man", is a plea of family: we come together because we are brothers. Rashbam and Radak read it exactly so; Sforno adds that if they were spies, a king would not choose ten sons of one man. Rashi hears something eerie: the spirit of holiness stirred in them, so that they included Joseph in "one man's sons" without knowing it, and the line is true of him as well.

The second is "honest" (kenim). The KJV's "true men" is acceptable though archaic. Rashi and Radak gloss kenim as "truthful", linked to ken, "so". The Hebrew insists on itself with the doubled pronouns, "we... we" (nachnu, anachnu), as a guilty-sounding protest; the actors should let it spill out too fast. Notice also the verb in the last clause is a past: "never were" your servants spies. Sforno and Ramban read it as "never, in all our lives".

philological_notes.note: 'Honest, upright, truthful': a word unusual in the Bible, appearing mostly in this story. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra link it to ken 'so, truly'. The link to a Hebrew root meaning 'to be firm' is a plausible reading but not certain.
'All of us sons of one man.' A defence from family; Rashi hears Joseph included unwittingly.

verses.translation_literal: And he said to them, "No! It is the nakedness of the land you have come to see."
verses.translation_dramatic: "No," he said. "No. It is the land's nakedness you have come to see."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph does not argue; he repeats. The same words as verse 9, with the object put first for emphasis: "the nakedness of the land you have come to see". It is the voice of a man who has decided not to be persuaded. Rashi preserves the rabbinic reasoning for the charge: you entered by ten different gates, and now you come together, as spies do; Sforno hears "No, you are not truly brothers" in the opening word; Rashbam says he is probing for whether Benjamin is alive.

The KJV's "Nay, but" correctly takes lo ki as the adversative "no, but". STEPBible's split of the words, "In-deed", is a mistake of the table, not of the sense; the particle is the plain "No, but". The play for the actors is the contrast with the humble tone of verse 10: now it is the Egyptian lord who says "no" to the Hebrew, and the brothers hear only the verdict.

philological_notes.note: 'No, but...': a flat denial of what was said, followed by the contrary statement. The STEPBible glosses split it as 'In-deed', which does not suit the context.

verses.translation_literal: And they said, Twelve [were] your servants, brothers [are] we, sons of one man in the land of Canaan; and behold, the small one [is] with our father today, and the one, he is not.
verses.translation_dramatic: They answered him, and their voices were low. "Twelve of us, my lord, your servants, brothers all, sons of a single man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is with our father this very day. And the other one..." A pause. "He is not."
verses.directors_commentary:
The brothers answer a charge of espionage with a family tree, because in the ancient Near East a man's identity was his house, and a house was hard to counterfeit. Spies travel alone or in unrelated crews; twelve sons of one father is a story that can be checked. Radak notes the brothers say 'sons of one man' precisely to make that point, and Sforno has them say it so the inquiry will confirm it.

The last words are the heart of the verse. The Hebrew says 've-ha-echad einennu', 'and the one, he is not', the same word 'ein' used for a vanished or no-longer-existing person. It is neither 'dead' nor 'alive'. BBE's 'one is dead' decides what the brothers carefully do not say; Radak reads the vagueness as deliberate, since they cannot claim to know. KJV 'one is not' is faithful here, though 'twelve brethren' in the first clause blurs the Hebrew, which has the number first and 'your servants' second: 'twelve [are] your servants'. Note, too, the irony the audience knows: the 'one who is not' is standing in front of them, and 'the small one' (ha-qatan) will become the whole plot.

philological_notes.note: 'He is not': the negative of existence with a pronoun suffix. It says nothing on whether the person is alive; it only says he is absent. The brothers' phrase can be a lie, a euphemism or an honest ignorance, and Radak takes the last of these.
'The small one', not 'the youngest' (KJV): the same word will return in vv. 15, 20 as the test of their story.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph said to them, It [is] that which I spoke to you, saying, Spies [are] you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph did not move. "It is as I told you," he said. "Spies. You are spies."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph hears a plain answer and refuses it. He does not argue the evidence; he repeats the charge, which is how an interrogator keeps the power. 'Hu asher dibbarti' is almost a shrug: 'it is exactly what I said.' The accusation closes a circle: whatever they say, it will confirm him.

The KJV 'That is it that I spake' is accurate if stiff. BBE's 'you have come with some secret purpose' replaces the single word 'meraggelim', 'spies', with a paraphrase, softening a charge that in Egypt carried the death penalty. Radak hears Joseph's logic: if the family is so loyal, why did not all twelve come? Sforno reads the 'one who is not' as a possible scout who has gone ahead. The play on the root 'regel', 'foot', in 'meraggelim', those who walk the land, was already pressed in v.9.

philological_notes.note: 'Spies', literally 'foot-men', those who walk over a country to see its weak places. The charge is the same word each time it is repeated in this scene (vv. 9, 11, 14, 16, 30).

verses.translation_literal: By this you will be tested: [by] the life of Pharaoh, if you go out from this [place]—except at the coming of your small brother here.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Here is how I will try you," said Joseph. "By the life of Pharaoh, you will not leave this place. Not one of you. Not until your youngest brother stands here before me."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph swears by the life of Pharaoh, which for an Egyptian official was the strongest oath there was, since Pharaoh was a god-king, and the oath sets the scene in Egypt rather than in the family's tradition. Rashi remarks dryly that a man swore by Pharaoh's life when he meant to lie; Joseph is not lying about the consequence, only about his stance.

The oath is a curse formula with the curse unspoken: 'if you go out from here' is the first half of a sentence whose second half ('may Pharaoh perish') is left to the imagination. KJV supplies a plain negative, 'ye shall not go forth', which is right in sense but loses that the Hebrew has a conditional hanging in the air. 'Tevachenu' ('you will be tested') uses the verb of assaying metals; the brothers are ore. Sforno explains the test: if they are not brothers, no young man will risk his life to come with liars. The little word 'hennah', 'here', is a pointed one: Joseph wants the youngest in this room, within reach.

philological_notes.note: 'By the life of Pharaoh', an oath formula with the king's life as the guarantee. Egyptian oaths by the king are attested; the biblical author uses it as local colour.
'You will be tested': assaying metal, a lab test, not a trial. The same root returns in v. 16.

verses.translation_literal: Send from you one, and let him take your brother, and you, be bound, and let your words be tested—[is] truth with you? And if not, [by] the life of Pharaoh, surely spies [are] you.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Send one of your number. Let him fetch your brother. The rest of you will wait in chains, and we shall see whether your words are true or only words. And if they are not, then by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies."
verses.directors_commentary:
The offer is a trap built like a bargain: one goes, nine stay. The structure is the one every hostage-taker uses, and the brothers will hear it as the sentence it is.

Three small things matter. First, 'ha-emet itkhem' opens with the interrogative he, a real question: 'is truth with you?' Rashi notes the pointing as a question, and Radak links it to the brothers' own claim, 'we are honest' (v. 11). KJV turns it into a purpose clause, 'whether there be any truth in you', which is serviceable. Second, 'be bound' (he'asoru) is an imperative: Joseph orders them to imprison themselves, a grim courtesy. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'you shall be bound'. Third, the oath is repeated, so the verse ends the way v. 14 did, with 'meraggelim attem'. BBE's 'your purpose is certainly secret' is a paraphrase that blunts the word 'spies'.

philological_notes.note: 'Be bound', a Niphal imperative: a command to submit to being bound. Ibn Ezra takes it as 'you shall be bound'.
'Is it truth?': a real question; Rashi says the he has patach because it is a question of doubt.

verses.translation_literal: And he gathered them into custody, three days.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he had them gathered up, all ten, and shut away in the guardhouse. One day. Two. Three.
verses.directors_commentary: Joseph does not take the offer he has just made. He lets them rot for three days first. 'Va-ye'esof' is 'and he gathered', the word for gathering harvest or herd: they are collected like goods. KJV 'put them all together' captures that; BBE's flat 'prison' loses the verb. 'Mishmar' is a holding place under guard, not a sentence; it is the same word Joseph himself knew as a prisoner in Potiphar's house (Gen 40:3). Ramban reads the three days as fear and a lever; Radak notes it was a discomfort that did not touch their bodies or goods. Three days is also the ordinary length of a journey or a crisis in the narrative, and the length of time the butler and baker waited in Gen 40.

philological_notes.note: 'Custody', a place of guarding. Rashi: the prison. Joseph's own prison in Gen 40 uses the same word.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph said to them on the third day, This do and live: the God I [am] fearing.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the third day Joseph came to them, and the terms had changed. "Do this, and you will live. I am a man who fears God."
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood shifts without warning. The man who swore by Pharaoh now says 'ha-Elohim', 'the God', and the brothers, who feared an Egyptian tyrant, are told their judge fears the same power they do. Radak and Sforno hear mercy here: the fear of God is why Joseph will not keep them all while their households starve.

The Hebrew puts the object first, 'et ha-Elohim ani yare', 'the God, I fear', which gives it the emphasis KJV's 'for I fear God' and BBE's 'I am a god-fearing man' soften into a plain justification. Using 'ha-Elohim' with the article, rather than YHWH, is how a foreign official could speak to foreigners and still be telling the truth. 'And live' is no comfort; it implies the alternative.

philological_notes.note: 'The God' with the article, put first for emphasis; the neutral name an Egyptian could say, and a speaker of any nation would recognize.

verses.translation_literal: If honest [are] you, your brother, one, let him be bound in the house of your custody; and you, go, bring grain of the hunger of your households.
verses.translation_dramatic: "If you are honest men, then let one brother stay bound in this house where you have been kept. The rest of you, go. Carry grain home, enough to meet the hunger in your houses."
verses.directors_commentary:
The terms soften and reverse: now only one stays and nine go, where in v. 16 nine stayed and one went. Joseph has turned the screw by lessening it, and the brothers are meant to feel the gift of that mercy.

'Kenim' is 'honest, upright', from the root of 'stand firm', and ties to 'ken' in v. 11, the word the brothers used of themselves; Radak notes it. KJV 'true men' is right; BBE's 'if you are true men' is loosely the same. 'Sheber' is grain, literally 'what is broken', i.e. what is bought to break hunger, as Radak explains with reference to Gen 41:56. KJV 'corn' is British for grain, not maize. 'Sheber ra'avon batteikhem' is a compressed phrase, 'grain of the hunger of your houses', i.e. the grain that answers your households' hunger, which Rashi spells out.

philological_notes.note: 'Grain', literally 'a breaking': what is bought to break the famine. Radak ties it to the verb for buying grain in Gen 41:56.
'Honest, upright'. The brothers used the word of themselves in v. 11; Joseph now sets a condition on it.

verses.translation_literal: And your small brother you will bring to me, and your words will be confirmed, and you will not die. And they did so.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And your youngest brother, bring him to me. Then your words will stand, and you will not die." They agreed, and it was done.
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph states the reward as a negative: 'you will not die'. In the world of this scene that is not a figure of speech. A court that has sworn by Pharaoh's life can execute spies, and Sforno adds the chilling point that Joseph could kill them in Canaan as well if they failed to return.

'Ye'amenu' ('will be confirmed') is the passive of the root of 'amen', 'to be firm, reliable'. Rashi glosses it by 'amen amen' and by 'let your word be confirmed' (1 Kings 8:26). KJV 'verified' is a fair rendering. 'Va-ya'asu-khen', 'and they did so', is a formula for obedience in the Torah, and it falls like a door closing. The brothers' acquiescence is as short as the text can make it.

philological_notes.note: 'May they be confirmed, proved reliable'; the same root as 'amen' and 'truth' (emet), tying back to v. 16's question.

verses.translation_literal: And they said, a man to his brother, Truly guilty [are] we concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul when he sought favor to us and we did not listen; therefore has come to us this distress.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then they spoke to one another, low, each to his brother. "We are guilty. Guilty, over our brother. We saw the anguish in him when he begged us, and we would not hear. That is why this distress has come on us."
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first time in the Joseph story that anyone says aloud what the brothers did. Notice what the original narrative in Gen 37 left out: the pleading. We learn it here, from the guilty. Ramban calls the omission deliberate, a story that tells the cruelty only when conscience does; Radak says Joseph begged as they stripped his tunic.

The Hebrew is rhythmic in sound and root: 'tsarat nafsho' ('distress of his soul') comes back as 'ha-tsarah ha-zot' ('this distress'). The brothers match measure for measure: the same word 'tsarah' names his pain then and theirs now, as Sforno and Rashbam see it. They think of the jail as a pit. KJV 'verily guilty' for 'aval ashemim' is good, though the particle 'aval' here is 'truly' (Rashi: Aramaic 'in truth'; Ibn Ezra compares Gen 17:19) and not the usual 'but'. The word 'nefesh' is not 'soul' in a modern sense but the whole self and throat, the life itself.

philological_notes.note: 'Truly, indeed': not the usual 'but'. Rashi cites the Aramaic translation 'in truth'; Ibn Ezra compares Gen 17:19.
'The distress of his self': the narrow place of the life; the same root returns as 'this tsarah' for the brothers' own plight, a measure-for-measure link.

verses.translation_literal: And Reuben answered them, saying, Did I not say to you, saying, Do not sin against the boy, and you did not listen? And also his blood, behold, is being required.
verses.translation_dramatic: Reuben answered them, bitter and tired. "Did I not tell you? Do not wrong the boy. And you would not listen. Now there it is: his blood is being asked for."
verses.directors_commentary:
Reuben, the firstborn who tried to rescue Joseph in Gen 37:22, has waited twenty years to say 'I told you so.' It is a cold sort of grief, which reaches for blame in the very moment of confession.

The Hebrew keeps the repetition 'saying... saying', and the sound play on 'shema'' ('hear/obey'): they did not listen then, and Joseph is listening now (v. 23). KJV 'child' for 'yeled' is fine; 'sin against the boy' keeps the moral weight that BBE's 'Do the child no wrong' dilutes. 'His blood is required' is a legal claim: in Israel's law, blood spilled is a debt that someone will seek, and 'nidrash' is the same root as 'darash', 'to seek out' (cf. Gen 9:5). Radak says they assumed Joseph dead; Sforno says a man who died as a slave is still blood on their hands. Rashi, reading the 'gam', makes it a hint of 'his blood and the old man's blood' as well.

philological_notes.note: 'Is being sought out, required': the verb of an avenger or judge demanding a debt of blood. Compare Gen 9:5.
'Do not sin': a moral word, not the milder 'do wrong'. The object is introduced by 'b-' (against).

verses.translation_literal: And they did not know that Joseph [was] hearing, for the interpreter [was] between them.
verses.translation_dramatic: They did not know that Joseph heard every word. Between them and him there had always been an interpreter, and so they thought the Egyptian could not understand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The narrator breaks in to tell us what the brothers cannot see: the Egyptian lord understands Hebrew. All the bitter confession was said in the language of the household, and the one person it was never meant for is listening.

'Shome'a' means 'hearing' and also 'understanding', as Rashi and Rashbam both note. The Hebrew repeats the 'ki' twice (that... for...), and the second explains the first: the interpreter's presence made them careless. 'Ha-melitz' is the go-between; the root also means 'to speak eloquently' and later 'mocker', which is why the word has a sly colour. KJV 'he spake unto them by an interpreter' is a reasonable gloss, though the Hebrew puts the interpreter 'between them' (beinotam) physically in the room. Rashi, following the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, calls him Manasseh, Joseph's son. That cannot be read from the Hebrew; the midrash is making the point that the family circle was already near.

philological_notes.note: 'The interpreter, go-between'. The sense of the root as 'speak for another' is the same as the later 'advocate'.
'Hearing' in the sense of understanding, since Joseph could follow Hebrew without needing translation.

verses.translation_literal: And he turned away from upon them and wept; and he returned to them and spoke to them; and he took from with them Simeon, and bound him to their eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph turned from them. He had to. He wept where they could not see. Then he came back, composed, and spoke to them once more. He chose Simeon from among them, and in front of their eyes, he had him bound.
verses.directors_commentary:
The most human moment of the scene happens offstage. Joseph's tears are rare in the Torah, and they mark each turn of his reunion. Rashi says he turned away so they would not see; he wept, says Rashi and Radak, because he heard that they were repenting.

Then he does the hard thing. Why Simeon? Rashi quotes two midrashim: he was the one who proposed throwing Joseph into the pit, or Joseph wished to part him from Levi, his partner at Shechem (Gen 34), lest the two plot together; Rashbam gives the second. Both are rabbinic explanations; the text is silent. The binding is done 'le-enehem', 'to their eyes', i.e. as a spectacle. Rashi, following Genesis Rabbah, says he was bound only in view of the brothers and fed and bathed once they left. KJV 'communed with them' for 'va-yedaber' is archaic; the Hebrew simply says 'and he spoke'. 'Va-ye'esor' ('and he bound') repeats the root of 'be bound' in v. 16 and 19, so the sentence is carried out in the same word in which it was offered.

philological_notes.note: 'To their eyes': before them, as a public act so that they must see it.
'And he wept': Joseph's first tears in the reunion; the verb of the narrator is unadorned.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph commanded, and they filled their vessels [with] grain, and to return their silver, each to his sack, and to give to them provision for the way; and [one] did for them thus.
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph gave his orders, quietly, as a man gives orders he means to be carried out and never spoken of. The brothers' vessels were filled to the brim with grain. Then came the other commands: each man's silver was to go back where it had come from, into his own sack, and food for the road was to be pressed into their hands. All of it was done exactly so.
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph is still playing the stern Egyptian official, and what he orders is the opposite of what his harshness would predict: free grain, the purchase money hidden again in the sacks, and travel rations on top. Nothing tells us why. Ramban reads the provisions as kindness, a way of showing them that he means no harm if their words prove true; the returned silver is the hook that will drag them back into fear. Play it as a man hiding tenderness inside a trap.

The Hebrew changes subject without warning. 'They filled' has no named agent (Radak: the servants who sold the grain) and 'did for them thus' is impersonal, so the KJV's 'and thus did he unto them' quietly makes Joseph do the work himself. 'Vessels' (kelim) is wider than 'sacks': the KJV narrows it. Note too the plural 'silvers' (kaspeihem), a point that bothered Ibn Ezra and Sforno, who explain it as separate coins. The grain is bar, the threshed kernel, a donkey-load of staple for a famine-stricken household.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'their silvers'. Silver was weighed out, not coined, so the plural is unusual; Ibn Ezra and Sforno discuss why a mass noun takes a plural here and settle on separate pieces or coins.
Travel provisions, food for the road; a variant spelling of the same word appears as tzeidah. Ramban takes the gift as the sign that Joseph wished no ill to them.

verses.translation_literal: And they lifted their grain upon their donkeys, and they went from there.
verses.translation_dramatic: They heaved the grain onto the backs of their donkeys, load upon patient load, and turned from that place. No one looked behind them.
verses.directors_commentary: A plain verse, and meant to be: the brothers are relieved, leaving with food and with one fewer brother than they came with, and the reader knows more than they do about what lies in the sacks. Ibn Ezra notes only that 'their grain' is what they bought, that is, they leave with the purchased goods and nothing more apparent. The donkey (hamor) is the beast of burden of the Canaan–Egypt caravan route; there is no camel train here, and a family's grain for a famine year is a serious weight. KJV 'laded' and 'thence' are merely archaic; the Hebrew is simple 'lifted' and 'from there'.

verses.translation_literal: And the one opened his sack to give fodder to his donkey at the lodging place, and he saw his silver, and behold, it [was] in the mouth of his sack.
verses.translation_dramatic: At the first night's halt, one of them loosened the neck of his sack to feed his donkey. And there, at the very mouth of it, where his hand went in, lay his silver. He stood and looked at it.
verses.directors_commentary:
Only one brother opens a sack here, and the text calls him simply 'the one' (ha'echad). Rashi, Radak and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan say he is Levi, left without Simeon, his partner in the massacre at Shechem; Ibn Ezra suggests Reuben, the firstborn, on the logic of 'one' as first in a count. The text names no one, so play him as any of them. Ramban and Radak both try to explain why only he found his money at this point and the others later (v35): Radak says Joseph arranged for one man's silver to sit at the mouth of the bag to unsettle them, the rest deeper; Ramban imagines a two-sided bag. These are the commentators' reconstructions, not the text.

The 'lodging place' (malon) is a night stop, perhaps a campsite or caravanserai; the KJV's 'inn' suggests a building with a roof. Misspo is the straw-and-barley fodder carried for the animals. The sack here is amtachat, and the silver is 'in its mouth', which makes the discovery immediate and inescapable: he did not have to dig. The KJV's 'espied' is a stagey word for a plain 'saw'.

philological_notes.note: A word for sack distinct from saq in the same verse. Rashi equates the two; Ramban distinguishes the amtachat as a larger two-sided bag, from the root 'to stretch', with Onkelos' Aramaic 'to'ana'.
A place to pass the night (root lun, 'to lodge'). Rashi: 'the place where they lodged for the night'.

verses.translation_literal: And he said to his brothers, My silver has been returned, and also, behold, [it is] in my sack! And their heart went out, and they trembled, each to his brother, saying, What [is] this [that] God has done to us?
verses.translation_dramatic: "My silver," he said to his brothers. "It has been given back. Look, it is here in my sack." And something went out of them: their hearts seemed to leave their bodies. They shook, and turned to one another, each to his brother, and the words came out in a whisper. "What is this? What has God done to us?"
verses.directors_commentary:
The brothers do not see an Egyptian prank; they see God's hand, and not a kind one. That is the weight of 'Elohim' here: they have been waiting for a reckoning for twenty years. Rashi hears the dread as fear of a pretext, that the silver was returned only so that they could be accused of theft; Rashbam, more theologically, reads it as measure for measure, and Sforno as the brothers fearing that Joseph's God-fearing ruler has been moved to enslave them in payment for the sale of their brother. The next chapter shows that fear in their mouths (43:18). The nicest line to play is the plain one: 'what is this?'

The idiom 'their heart went out' (vayyetze libbam) is flat and physical, and the KJV 'failed them' smooths it into a figure. Radak compares Song of Songs 5:6, 'my soul went out when he spoke'. The ASV's 'turned trembling' is a fair rendering of vayyecheredu, 'they trembled'. 'Hushav' is passive: the silver 'was returned', by no one the speaker can name.

philological_notes.note: 'Their heart went out': the heart leaves its place in a shock of fear. Radak links it to Song of Songs 5:6.
To tremble, to shake with dread; the verb of the helpless, as in Isaac's trembling at Genesis 27:33.

verses.translation_literal: And they came to Jacob their father, [to] the land of Canaan, and they told him all the things that had befallen them, saying:
verses.translation_dramatic: They came home at last, to Jacob their father in the land of Canaan, and they laid it all out for him, everything that had happened to them on the road and in Egypt. They began to speak:
verses.directors_commentary: The Hebrew puts weight on 'all that happened to them' (kol hakkorot otam), from the root qarah, 'to meet, to befall': what happened to them is told as a series of chance events, as something that came upon them, which is how brothers who are hiding a very different old story would choose to tell it. Radak notes that the account they give Jacob is summarized and differs in details from the earlier scene, though the substance is the same. 'Came to Jacob... to the land of Canaan' is a stumbling phrase in Hebrew as in English; the KJV's doubled 'unto' follows it closely. The ending 'saying' hands us straight into the report, whose slant deserves attention in the next verses.

philological_notes.note: 'The things that befell': from qarah, 'to meet, to happen', often used for what comes by chance or from God. Radak observes that the retelling to Jacob contains additions, omissions and changes while the substance is the same.

verses.translation_literal: The man, the lord of the land, spoke with us [things] hard, and he made us like spies of the land.
verses.translation_dramatic: The man who is lord of that country spoke to us hard, hard words. He took us, he set us down, as men who had come to spy out the land.
verses.directors_commentary: The brothers begin their report by blaming the Egyptian, and they use his title with care: 'the man, the lord of the land' (ha'ish adonei ha'aretz). Adonei is plural in form, a plural of majesty, which the KJV renders 'the lord'. They never name him, since they do not know him. 'Spoke hard things with us' is a real Hebrew idiom: qashot is 'hard things', left without its noun, and Onkelos and Pseudo-Jonathan supply 'words'. KJV 'spake roughly' is right. BBE's 'put us in prison' is not in the verse (that is later, v17); the Hebrew says only that he 'set us as spies', that is, treated us as such. Play it as the brothers rehearsing the facts that will make Jacob sympathetic: they were falsely accused.

philological_notes.note: 'Like spies': from regel, 'foot', so the spy is one who goes about on foot. The Targums render 'like those who search out the land'.

verses.translation_literal: And we said to him, True men [are] we; we have not been spies.
verses.translation_dramatic: And we answered him. We said: We are honest men. We have never been spies.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the brothers quote themselves to their father, and the word they quote is the one that trapped them. Kenim ("true, straight, honest") is the brothers' own word from 42:11, where they protested "kenim anachnu", "we are true men", to the man in charge of Egypt's grain. Joseph picked it up and turned it into his condition: "if you are kenim" (42:19), and "then I will know that you are kenim" (42:33-34). Now they repeat it to Jacob as if it were a plain statement of character. Played well, it is a defence that has already cost them a brother in prison. Say it as men who are still being tested by it.

The KJV's "true men" and "no spies" are sound, though "we be" and "no spies" are archaic padding; the Hebrew says "we have not been spies" (lo hayinu), a flat denial about the past. BBE's "we have no evil designs" softens the accusation, and loses the repeated word: the charge was spying, meraggelim, a participle built from regel, "foot", men who go on foot over the land to see where it is weak. The accusation was about feet on ground, and the answer is about character. Onkelos renders kenim as "upright" and Pseudo-Jonathan as "trustworthy", both reading it as a moral claim, not a mere denial.

philological_notes.note: "Straight, true, honest". It is the brothers' own claim in 42:11, which Joseph turned into the standard of his test (42:19, 33-34). Here they hand it back to Jacob, so the word travels through the whole episode like a charge on a ledger. The KJV's "true men" hides that it is the same word each time only if a reader does not look for it.

"Spies", literally those who go about on the foot (regel); a participle of the same root as "foot". The word is repeated from Joseph's charge in 42:9-16, so the brothers deny precisely what was alleged.

verses.translation_literal: Two ten [are] we, brothers, sons of our father: the one [is] not, and the small one [is] this day with our father in the land of Canaan.
verses.translation_dramatic: We are twelve brothers, sons of one father. One of us is no more. And the youngest is at home today, there with our father in the land of Canaan.
verses.directors_commentary:
The brothers lay out their family for Jacob as they did before Joseph (42:13), and the speech is built to stop on its last words: the youngest, with our father, in Canaan. It is the one fact that will bring the demand for Benjamin, so let the line fall quietly. Nothing in the verse gives the brothers' reason for it, and nothing should be added.

The Hebrew says "two ten", the ordinary way to say twelve; the number matters because twelve sons are the household, and the verse counts them down to a hole. "The one is not" (ha'echad eineinu) is the text's own phrase, bare and without a cause. The KJV keeps "one is not", which is right. BBE's "one is dead" supplies a death the Hebrew does not state, and Pseudo-Jonathan glosses it as "we do not know what became of him". The brothers who sold Joseph speak these words to the father who mourns him, so the phrase carries what they know and cannot say. Note too that the KJV's "the youngest" is hakaton, "the small one": the same word that marks a child, here a grown man, still thought of as his father's little boy. "This day" (hayom) comes before the preposition and stresses the present moment: today, at least, he is safe.

philological_notes.note: "The one is not". The word ayin ("there is not") with a suffix, a flat statement of absence that says nothing about how or why. BBE's "is dead" and the KJV's silence differ here: the Hebrew leaves open what the brothers mean and what they know.
"The small one", the youngest. The KJV's "youngest" is a fair rendering; the Hebrew simply says "small", which in a family context carries the sense of the baby of the household.

verses.translation_literal: And the man, the lord of the land, said to us, By this I will know that you [are] honest: your brother, the one, leave with me, and the hunger of your households take, and go.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the lord of that land said to us, "Here is how I shall know you are honest men. Leave one of your brothers with me. Take what your houses need against the hunger, and go."
verses.directors_commentary: The brothers quote Joseph's test (42:19–20) in the most reasonable terms they can. 'The hunger of your households' (ra'avon bateichem) is a compressed phrase: Radak and Ibn Ezra explain it as grain for the hunger, 'what your households need'. The KJV 'the famine of your households' gives the Hebrew literally but lets the sentence stumble. The Aramaic Targums supply 'grain'. The whole speech is the brothers speaking: they do not say that Joseph put Simeon in bonds in front of them (42:24), and Ramban notes they leave out the imprisonment. The closing 'take and go' (qechu valechu) is a dismissal.

philological_notes.note: 'Hunger' (a rare noun); here by metonymy the grain that answers it. Radak: 'the grain for the hunger of your households.'

verses.translation_literal: And bring your brother, the youngest, to me, and let me know that you [are] not spies, that you [are] honest. Your brother I will give to you, and the land you will go about [in trade].
verses.translation_dramatic: "Bring me your youngest brother. Then I shall know you are no spies but honest men. Then I will give your brother back to you, and you may move freely through this land, buying and selling as you please."
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hook, repeated by the brothers to Jacob so that he will hear the price of his sons' release: Benjamin. They add a promise Joseph did not make in the scene we have: 'and you will go about the land'. Ramban notes the text does not record it and guesses Joseph said it to sweeten the demand, or that the brothers softened it to persuade their father; either way, it is the brothers' bargaining chip. The verb tiscaharu comes from the root of the word for merchant and for 'going about': Rashi derives sochrim, 'merchants', from the way they travel around after goods. The KJV's 'traffick' meant 'trade' in 1611 and now reads as something sinister; the modern word is 'trade'. 'Deliver' for natan (give) is also too formal.

philological_notes.note: 'You will go about, trade': the root gives sochar, 'merchant' and sechorah, 'merchandise', from circulating. Rashi explains the whole family of words by 'going around after goods'. Ramban prefers a milder sense, freedom to buy grain, and compares Genesis 34:10.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, they [were] emptying their sacks, and behold, each man's bag of silver [was] in his sack; and they saw the bags of their silver, they and their father, and they were afraid.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then, as they were emptying the sacks, there it was: each man's silver, tied up in its own small bag, lying in the grain. They saw it, the brothers and their father together, and every one of them was afraid.
verses.directors_commentary: The second discovery, and it is the whole company this time: every man's silver in his own bundle (tzeror), tied up as it had been when he paid. The detail 'they and their father' (hemmah va'avihem) matters: Jacob sees what his sons saw, and the fear is now a family's. Radak gives the reason for the dread: someone has given back the money in order to trap them, so that they could be held as thieves. Rashi glosses tzeror simply as a knot, 'the tying-up of his silver'. Notice also the small difference from v27: there the silver was 'in the mouth of the sack', here 'in the sack'; Radak notes the brothers say 'in his sack' rather than 'mouth of his sack', and gives his reason. KJV 'bundle' is fine; BBE 'parcel' too.

philological_notes.note: A bundle or bag tied up, a knotted purse; Rashi: 'the tying of his silver'. The same root as 'to bind'.
'Emptying' (hiphil participle of riq, 'empty'), a vivid present: the discovery comes in the very act of unloading.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob their father said to them, Me you have made childless: Joseph [is] not, and Simeon [is] not, and Benjamin you would take; upon me are they, all of them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Jacob, their father, answered them. "Me. It is me you have robbed of my children. Joseph is gone. Simeon is gone. And now you would take Benjamin as well. It all comes down on me."
verses.directors_commentary: The emphatic word comes first: 'Me!' (oti), set before the verb, a cry of wounded fatherhood. Shikkaltem, 'you have bereaved', comes from shakol, the language of a parent whose children are lost; Rashi says it describes anyone whose sons are gone, and that Jacob also suspects the brothers of having killed or sold Joseph; Radak takes it as 'you have brought all these troubles on me'. Jacob lists his losses as a drumbeat, with 'is not' (einennu) twice, the same flat euphemism the brothers used in v32. The KJV 'all these things are against me' catches the rare ending of kullanah, 'all of them', which Ibn Ezra and Radak explain as 'all these troubles'. Sforno hears the sharper point: such misfortunes would not strike a household unless its sons were quarrelling with one another. For the actor, there is nothing historical to explain; this is simply an old man at his lowest.

philological_notes.note: 'You have made childless': the bereavement verb, here in the piel with Jacob as the one robbed. Rashi: anyone whose sons are lost is called a shakkul. Radak compares 1 Samuel 15:33 (your sword made women childless).
'All of them': a feminine plural suffix on kol, which Ibn Ezra and Radak read as 'all these troubles'.

verses.translation_literal: And Reuben said to his father, saying: [Of] my two sons you may put to death if I do not bring him to you. Give him upon my hand, and I, I will bring him back to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Reuben spoke, and his voice was steady, though there was little behind it but his own two sons. "Kill my sons," he said to his father, "both of them, if I do not bring him back to you. Put him in my hand. Put him in my hand, and I will bring him home to you again."
verses.directors_commentary:
Reuben, the firstborn, last spoke in 42:22, reminding his brothers of their guilt over Joseph, and he now stakes the one thing he can offer: his sons. This is a self-imprecation, close to an oath-penalty: the sons are surety, as property and heirs would be in ancient Near Eastern pledge and guarantee law. The phrase 'upon my hand' (עַל־יָדִי) is a custody idiom: the person is placed into the keeping of the guarantor. Reuben is not offering a grisly bargain so much as the strongest legal formula available. Note the emphasis in 'and I, I' (וַאֲנִי): the Hebrew puts the pronoun on the front of the verb, and the line is a promise made by the very son who once failed his father (Gen 35:22, 37:21-22, 29).

The KJV 'Slay my two sons' is accurate in force but flattens the structure; 'deliver him' turns a plain 'give' (תְּנָה) into legal-sounding English, and 'again' (for 'back') is archaic. The Hebrew uses the root שׁוב ('return') in the last verb, which sets up the whole following story: Benjamin must be brought back, not merely brought. Ramban notes that Reuben says 'two' sons although he had four, as a doubling of a single loss; Radak reports that Jacob thought it a foolish thing to say, and Rashi on v.38 repeats the midrash that Jacob called him a foolish firstborn: 'are they your sons and not mine?' That is the audience's reaction in the room: the offer lands as noise, not comfort.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil 'cause to die', 'put to death'. Here it is a penalty Reuben invites on himself if he fails; the same pledge is later made by Judah in 43:9 and 44:32 with a different formula ('I shall have sinned against you all my days').
Literally 'upon my hand': entrust him into my custody, make me answerable for him.

verses.translation_literal: And he said: My son will not go down with you, for his brother is dead and he, he alone, is left. And harm will befall him on the road on which you go, and you will bring down my gray hair in sorrow to Sheol.
verses.translation_dramatic: But Jacob would not be moved. "My son will not go down with you," he said. "His brother is dead. He is the one that is left, he alone. If harm should meet him on the road you travel, you will bring my white head down in sorrow to Sheol."
verses.directors_commentary:
Jacob's refusal is not stubbornness for its own sake. He speaks of Benjamin as the only remaining son of Rachel: 'his brother is dead' is Joseph, and 'he alone is left' (לְבַדּוֹ נִשְׁאָר) collapses two losses into one boy. Sforno underlines that Benjamin is the only one left from that beloved wife. Radak adds the human logic: if Joseph were alive, Jacob would have listened. The sentence is an old man's grief speaking as logic, and he refuses to bargain with Reuben, whose record includes Bilhah (Gen 35:22).

The KJV makes this sound mild. 'Mischief' (for אָסוֹן) is archaic and trivial in modern ears; the Hebrew word is a grave calamity, a rare word that suggests fatal harm.'The grave' for שְׁאוֹלָה quietly turns Sheol, the shadowy underworld of the dead, into a burial hole; and 'gray hairs' are in fact a single collective noun, 'my grey hair', his old age. The final verb is the same root as Jacob's 'go down' (ירד) in the opening line: Benjamin will not go down, but his father will be brought down. Ancient audiences would hear that echo as a threat: a long journey to Egypt in a famine is exactly where harm falls, and elderly fathers in a clan economy depend on the heir.

philological_notes.note: Rare word for fatal harm or calamity; appears only in Genesis 42:4, 42:38, 44:29 and Exodus 21:22-23. KJV's 'mischief' is an archaic and weak choice.
'My grey hair', a collective singular for the whole of old age; cf. Genesis 44:29, 31.
Sheol with directional ה: 'down to Sheol'. The realm of the dead, not simply a grave.

events.title: Jacob sends his sons to buy grain in Egypt
events.narrative_summary: Jacob sees that there is grain in Egypt and asks his sons why they stand looking at one another. He tells them to go down and buy, so that they may live and not die.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word in the text. Anchored on the START of Joseph's sales to the world (41:56-57) with an offset of 3 months and a margin of 2 months, so the start stays inside the second famine year. Gen 45:6 says only two famine years had passed at the reveal, and the first descent, the eating of its grain (43:2), the second descent and the reveal must all fit before that year ends. The tier is REGNAL_YEAR as the scene falls under the years of famine.

events.title: Ten brothers go down to Egypt; Benjamin stays
events.narrative_summary: Ten of Joseph's brothers go down to buy grain among the other travellers, because famine holds in Canaan. Jacob keeps Benjamin back for fear of harm.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when Jacob finishes speaking: 'And Joseph's ten brethren went down' (42:3). Duration 15 days from `urim travel loc.hebron loc.egypt --mode donkey`: 394 km straight, about 493 km by road, 4 km/h, about 32 km a day with laden donkeys. Jacob's home is Hebron (37:14; 35:27). Margin 3 days for Joseph's unnamed city.
events.ancient_season_marker: Famine in the land of Canaan

events.title: The brothers bow before Joseph, who knows them
events.narrative_summary: Joseph, ruler of the land and seller of its grain, sees his brothers bow with their faces to the ground. He recognizes them, but they do not recognize him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Anchored on the end of the journey: they arrive and come before him. A margin of two days covers the time to reach the city and to reach Joseph in the queue of buyers. Duration is the length of the audience's opening.

events.title: Joseph accuses his brothers of spying
events.narrative_summary: Joseph speaks harshly through an interpreter and charges them with being spies come to see the land's weakness. They protest that they are honest sons of one man, twelve brothers, and he insists, demanding that the youngest be brought to prove their words.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continuous with the audience in 42:6-8, with no marked gap, hence anchored on its end with no offset. About an hour for the exchange (42:9-16).

events.title: Joseph puts the brothers in custody for three days
events.narrative_summary: Joseph gathers them all into ward for three days.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Three days' (42:17) counted inclusively, as the first day (the arrest day) through the third day, when Joseph speaks (42:18): two full days of 24 hours from the end of the accusation to the third-day speech. The margin is 12 hours, as for the third-day speech, since no hour is given. It starts the moment the accusation ends; the custody then ends with the terms on day three.

events.title: Joseph offers new terms on the third day
events.narrative_summary: On the third day Joseph says he fears God and tells them to leave one brother in custody and carry grain home, then bring the youngest brother to him. They agree.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'On the third day' (42:18), counted inclusively with the first day of custody as day one, so START of the ward plus 2 days, margin 12 hours. No hour is given.

events.title: The brothers confess guilt for Joseph; Reuben rebukes them
events.narrative_summary: Speaking in Hebrew among themselves, the brothers say they are guilty for what they did to their brother, who pleaded with them. Reuben reminds them he told them not to sin against the boy. They do not know Joseph understands, since he used an interpreter.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows 'and they did so' (42:20) without any marked gap, so anchored on the end of the terms. A short exchange.

events.title: Joseph weeps, then binds Simeon before their eyes
events.narrative_summary: Joseph turns away and weeps, comes back and speaks to them, then takes Simeon from them and binds him in front of them.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Immediately after the confession, with Joseph hearing it, so anchored on the end of the confession with no offset.

events.title: Joseph has the sacks filled, the silver returned, and the brothers depart
events.narrative_summary: Joseph orders their vessels filled with grain, each man's silver put back in his sack, and provision given for the road. The brothers load their donkeys and leave.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continues straight on from the binding (a command, then its execution). Three hours to fill and load; no time of day is given, so the margin is half a day.

events.title: One brother finds his silver in his sack at the inn
events.narrative_summary: At a lodging place one brother opens his sack to feed his donkey and sees his silver in its mouth. He tells his brothers, and their hearts fail them as they ask what God has done to them.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'At the lodging place' (42:27) implies the first night or so on the road, so offset 1 day after the departure, margin 1 day. The packet gives no stops on the route, so the number is a guess.

events.title: The brothers report everything to Jacob
events.narrative_summary: The brothers reach Jacob in Canaan and tell him all that befell them: the lord of the land spoke harshly, held them as spies, and demanded their youngest brother, keeping one behind.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Offset 15 days from the end of the departure, the same donkey journey as the descent (`urim travel loc.hebron loc.egypt --mode donkey`, 493 km by road, 32 km a day; Jacob is at Hebron, 37:14). Margin 3 days. The tier is REGNAL_YEAR because the time rests on the famine-year frame, not on a day count in the text.

events.title: The sacks are emptied and every man's silver is found
events.narrative_summary: As they empty their sacks, each man finds his bundle of silver in his sack. Both they and their father see the bundles and are afraid.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'As they emptied their sacks' (42:35) follows the report with no gap. Anchored on the end of the report; margin one day for unpacking.

events.title: Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go, despite Reuben's pledge
events.narrative_summary: Jacob laments that his sons have bereaved him: Joseph is gone, Simeon is gone, and now they would take Benjamin. Reuben offers his own two sons as a pledge, but Jacob says Benjamin will not go down, lest harm bring his gray hairs down to Sheol in sorrow.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Jacob's answer to the silver and to the demand, in the same scene as the unpacking; anchored on its end, no offset.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Joseph's dream that his brothers' sheaves bow to his sheaf (37:7) comes true when the brothers bow with faces to the ground before him (42:6), and he recalls the dreams at 42:9.
Because Joseph sells grain to all the earth (41:56-57), Jacob hears there is grain in Egypt and sends his sons (42:1-2).
Recognizing his brothers and remembering his dreams (42:8-9), Joseph presents himself as a stranger and charges them with spying.
Jacob's command to go down and buy grain (42:2) is what sends the ten brothers to Egypt (42:3).
Joseph's terms (42:19) let him bind one brother as a hostage while the rest return with grain (42:24).
The report of Joseph's demand for Benjamin and the silver found in the sacks (42:29-35) makes Jacob refuse to send him (42:36-38).
Joseph's command to restore every man's silver into his sack (42:25) is why one brother finds his money at the lodging place (42:27-28).
The silver Joseph had put back into each sack (42:25) is what every man finds as they empty them at home (42:35).
The spy charge and Joseph's demand for proof lead him to lock them all up for three days (42:16-17).

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew kesef, 'silver', the common medium of payment.
entities.summary_bio: The silver with which the brothers paid for grain, which Joseph orders secretly put back into each man's sack. Its discovery at the lodging and at home fills them and their father with fear.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'son of the right hand' or 'son of the south'; his dying mother had called him Ben-oni, 'son of my sorrow' (Gen 35:18).
entities.summary_bio: Youngest son of Jacob and Rachel and full brother of Joseph. Jacob keeps him at home after Joseph's loss, fearing harm will befall him, and he becomes the test Joseph sets for his brothers.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew melits, 'one who interprets or mediates between speakers'.
entities.summary_bio: An unnamed go-between who stands between Joseph and his brothers, so that they do not suspect he understands Hebrew. His presence shows that Joseph, speaking as an Egyptian official, is unrecognised.

entities.etymology_meaning: Folk etymology in Gen 29:33: 'the LORD has heard'; from the root shama', 'to hear'.
entities.summary_bio: Second son of Jacob and Leah. Joseph binds him before his brothers' eyes and keeps him in Egypt as surety that they will return with Benjamin.

components.evidence_explanation: 42:4: Jacob did not send Benjamin with his brothers.
42:8: Joseph knew his brothers, but they did not know him.
42:21: 'we are guilty concerning our brother', recalling his pleas.
42:17: he put them into custody for three days; on the third day he speaks to them (42:18).
42:25: Joseph ordered each man's silver returned to his sack.
42:24: Joseph took Simeon from them and bound him before their eyes.

systems.name: Accusation of espionage
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Foreign visitors to a border or capital in a time of famine could be suspected of scouting weak points; Egypt's eastern frontier was watched against Asiatic incursions.
rules_and_mechanics: Strangers arriving from the border are suspected of surveying the land's 'nakedness', its weak points.
The accused must prove honesty by evidence, here by producing the missing brother.
Detention may be used while the claim is tested.

systems.name: Sale of grain in famine
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Egyptian granaries under state control sold stored grain to foreigners and natives in famine years, as in Joseph's administration (Gen 41:56).
rules_and_mechanics: Grain is sold for silver by the official in charge.
Buyers load their own animals and take provisions for the journey.
Foreign buyers come in numbers from afar, 'among those coming'.

systems.name: Hostage as surety
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Holding one person of a party as security for the return of another or the performance of terms is attested in treaties and trade across the region.
rules_and_mechanics: One member stays in custody while the others carry out the terms.
The hostage is released only when the terms are met.
Breach of terms puts the hostage at risk.

systems.name: Obeisance before a superior
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Bowing with the face to the ground was the standard act of homage before kings, officials and benefactors across the ancient Near East, and in Egyptian court art.
rules_and_mechanics: The inferior bows low, face to the ground, before the one whose favour is sought.
It is addressed to rank, whether or not the superior is recognised.
Petitioners call themselves 'servants' and the superior 'my lord'.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The brothers bow to the ground before Joseph, ruler of the land.
system_instances.significance_note: The bow answers the sheaf dream (37:7), in which the brothers' sheaves bowed to Joseph's; Joseph remembers that dream in 42:9. The star dream (37:9) is not yet fulfilled here.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The brothers' vessels are filled with grain, their silver put back, and provisions given.
system_instances.significance_note: The hidden silver is a quiet kindness that also fills the brothers with fear.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph swears by the life of Pharaoh that they will not leave unless their youngest brother comes.
system_instances.significance_note: It gives his demand the weight of an oath by the king he serves.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph has Simeon bound before them and kept as surety.
system_instances.significance_note: Simeon's detention compels a return, and with Benjamin, which drives the next chapters.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph insists they are spies and names a test, that their youngest brother must come.
system_instances.significance_note: The pretext lets Joseph learn whether Benjamin lives and how his brothers have changed.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph puts all ten brothers into custody for three days.
system_instances.significance_note: It lets them feel what Joseph felt in the pit, and prepares their confession.

edges.description: The brothers tell Jacob everything that had happened to them in Egypt.
Jacob says his sons have bereaved him, with Joseph and Simeon gone and Benjamin about to be taken.
Jacob rejects Reuben's pledge and will not let Benjamin go down, fearing he would die of grief.
Jacob tells his sons to go down to Egypt and buy grain so that the family may live.
Joseph tells his brothers they are spies come to see the land's weakness.
Joseph takes Simeon from the group and binds him before their eyes.
Joseph swears by Pharaoh's life that they cannot leave unless their youngest brother comes.
Joseph places all the brothers in custody for three days.
Joseph commands the brothers' vessels filled with grain, their silver returned, and provisions given for the road.
Reuben offers his own two sons as a pledge for Benjamin's safe return.
Reuben reminds his brothers that he warned them not to sin against the boy, and that his blood is now required.
